---
title: "09_pca"
format: html
---

## Aim

Run a PCA on the number of mutations in the top 20 genes of each sample, to
see whether cancer types or survival status form clusters, and identify genes 
that are associated to particular types of cancer

## Load libraries

```{r}
#| message: false

library("tidyverse")
library("here")
```


## Load data

```{r}
load(here("data", "03_cancer_augment.RData"))
```

## Extract the mutation matrix

```{r}
mutation_matrix <- clinical_augment |>
  select(starts_with("num_mut_"))
```

We then scale all genes so that each one has the same weight, whatever its
mutation frequency. It is a criticable approach, as we selected the top 20 genes
on their mutation frequency. But it also avoids genes very often mutated such as
TP53 to take too much importance in the analysis

```{r}
pca_fit <- mutation_matrix |>
  prcomp(center = TRUE,
         scale. = TRUE)
```

## Variance explained

```{r}
pca_variance <- tibble(pc = seq_along(pca_fit$sdev),
                       variance = pca_fit$sdev^2) |>
  mutate(pct_variance = variance / sum(variance) * 100)

pca_variance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pc,
             y = pct_variance)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Principal component",
       y = "Variance explained (%)",
       title = "Variance explained by each principal component")
```

```{r}
# PCA scores

pca_scores <- clinical_augment |>
  select(patient_id, cancer_type, status, total_mutations) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(pca_fit$x))

pc1_label <- str_c("PC1 (", round(pca_variance$pct_variance[1], 1), "%)")
pc2_label <- str_c("PC2 (", round(pca_variance$pct_variance[2], 1), "%)")
```

### Results colored by cancer type

```{r}
pca_scores |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1,
             y = PC2,
             color = cancer_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = pc1_label,
       y = pc2_label,
       color = "Cancer type",
       title = "PCA of mutation counts in the top 20 genes")
```

### Results colored by survival status

```{r}
pca_scores |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1,
             y = PC2,
             color = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = pc1_label,
       y = pc2_label,
       color = "Survival status",
       title = "PCA of mutation counts in the top 20 genes")
```
The PCA clearly doesn't separate patients based on their survival status. As we
could expect it, only the number of mutations per gene is not enough information
to predict the severity of a cancer. 

It doesn't clearly separate cancer types neither, especially the first component.
But the second component seems to show a partial separation of melanoma and 
colorectal cancer. Let's verify it with a box plot:

```{r}
# Box plot of PC2 in melanoma vs colorectal cancer

pc2_subset <- pca_scores |>
  filter(cancer_type %in% c("Melanoma", "Colorectal Cancer"))

pc2_test <- wilcox.test(PC2 ~ cancer_type,
                        data = pc2_subset)

pc2_test

pc2_subset |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cancer_type,
             y = PC2,
             fill = cancer_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Cancer type",
       y = "PC2",
       title = "PC2 in melanoma vs colorectal cancer",
       subtitle = str_c("Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = ",
                        format.pval(pc2_test$p.value,
                                    digits = 3)))
```
Indeed, melanoma have a greater PC2 value than colorectal cancer overall, and
the extremely small p-value of our test confirms significance. We can then
investigate the genes that drive PC2 most

## Genes driving PC2

```{r}
pca_loadings <- pca_fit$rotation |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "gene") |>
  select(gene, PC2) |>
  mutate(gene = str_remove(gene, "num_mut_")) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(PC2)))

pca_loadings
```

KRAS, TERT and APC are the genes driving PC2 most. It suggests that those genes
have a role either in melanoma or colorrectal cancer .Plotting a heatmap would
allow to verify those hypothesises

## Heatmap of top 20 Driver Genes

```{r}
# Load the augmented data
load(here("data", "03_cancer_augment.RData"))

# Reshape to long format and calculate mutation percentage per cancer type
heatmap_data <- clinical_augment |>
  # Gather all 20 num_mut_* columns into two columns: 'gene' and 'mut_count'
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("num_mut_"),
    names_to = "gene",
    values_to = "mut_count"
  ) |>
  # Clean up the gene names by removing the "num_mut_" prefix
  mutate(gene = str_remove(gene, "^num_mut_")) |>
  # Group by cancer type and gene
  group_by(cancer_type, gene) |>
  # Calculate the % of samples in that cancer type that have at least 1 mutation
  summarise(
    n_samples = n(),
    n_mutated = sum(mut_count > 0),
    pct_mutated = (n_mutated / n_samples) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```


```{r}
heatmap_data |>
  # Order genes so the most frequently mutated ones appear at the top
  mutate(gene = fct_reorder(gene, pct_mutated, .fun = mean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cancer_type, y = gene, fill = pct_mutated)) +
  # Draw the heatmap tiles with thin white borders
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Add exact percentage numbers inside the tiles
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct_mutated, 0)), size = 2.8, color = "black") +
  # Use a clean color gradient from light to dark
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#f7fbff",
    high = "#08519c",
    name = "Mutated\nSamples (%)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mutation Frequency of Top 20 Driver Genes Across Cancer Types",
    subtitle = "Values inside tiles indicate percentage (%) of samples with ≥1 mutation",
    x = "Cancer Type",
    y = "Driver Gene"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```
Indeed, KRAS and APC mutations appear to be correlated with colorectal cancer,
while TERT mutations seem correlated with melanoma. Even though the PCA is not 
very informative, because mutations alone don't carry enough biological context,
it allowed to draft hypothesises and confirm them with the heatmap.
